title: Tropical Storm Lala Batters Hawaii with Torrential Rain and Power Outages
summary:
Hawaii is reeling from Tropical Storm Lala, which weakened from a hurricane but continues to unleash devastating rain and wind across the islands. As of Sunday morning, more than 130,000 households were without power, and at least one person died in a car accident on the Big Island. The storm, centered about 105 miles west-northwest of Kailua-Kona, is expected to dump up to 35 inches of rain on higher slopes, causing flash floods and mudslides.

Governor Josh Green reported that 19 roofs were lost and roads have been severely impacted. Search-and-rescue teams, including the National Guard and Coast Guard, are looking for people after flash floods swept homes off their foundations in the coastal communities of Na'alehu and Wai'ohinu. "There's rushing water, debris, and boulders on the road and it's dark," said Hawaii County Mayor Kimo Alameda, describing the challenges.

Residents are bracing for more. Bobby Camara, 75, said he planned to "hunker down, cross my fingers, hope the lights don't go out." Mike Caputo, a fire captain in Keaau, is worried about falling albizia trees, which he says "can make roads impassable." The storm is moving west, with tropical storm warnings in effect for Maui, Oahu, Kauai, and other islands. Forecasters expect Lala to regain hurricane strength midweek after passing the island chain.

This is the second major weather disaster for Hawaii this year, following devastating floods in March. The state's rugged terrain and isolated communities make rescue efforts difficult. As the storm continues, authorities are urging residents to stay indoors and avoid flooded roads. The full extent of the damage won't be known until the rain stops and crews can reach remote areas.
why_it_matters: The storm shows how isolated island communities face outsized risk from extreme weather, and why emergency systems like the National Guard matter. For young people in coastal states, this is a reminder of how climate-driven storms can change daily life and shape public policy.

background_read: Tropical Storm Lala is part of the Pacific hurricane season, when warm ocean water can spin up storms that threaten Hawaii.
Hawaii is a U.S. island state in the central Pacific, and its remote location makes disaster response harder because supplies and crews often have to arrive by air or sea.

The Big Island, officially called Hawaii Island, is the largest and youngest island in the chain; Kailua-Kona is a town on its western side, while Na'alehu and Wai'ohinu are small coastal communities on the southern end.
The National Guard and Coast Guard mentioned in the search are military and maritime agencies that states call on for rescues during floods and hurricanes.

Albizia trees, an invasive species in Hawaii, are known for being fragile and dangerous in high winds because they can break apart and block roads, and many residents are already familiar with storm damage because this is Hawaii's second major weather disaster this year.

perspectives.description: The National Guard and Coast Guard are conducting search-and-rescue missions, and many residents are taking precautions by hunkering down. Warnings and early reports help communities prepare for the worst. This shows the value of coordinated emergency response.

Homes were swept off their foundations, roofs were lost, and at least one person died. The dark, debris-filled roads make rescues dangerous and slow. For a state already hit by March floods, this is another painful blow.

Tropical Storm Lala weakened from a hurricane but is forecast to regain strength after passing the islands. Hawaii's rugged terrain and isolated communities make recovery especially hard. Invasive albizia trees add an infrastructure risk that is unique to the region.

The full damage will remain unknown until crews reach remote areas. Forecasters are watching whether Lala regains hurricane strength midweek. Longer term, the state may need stronger tree management and better access routes for future storms.
